title: Lesson 8: Marriage and Relationships
description: Marriage is not finding a finished statue. It is two people who see what Jesus is making in each other and trust each other with the chisel. You will see the covenant love God gives first, how Christ's love for His church shapes marriage in Ephesians 5, and why drawing near to God draws two people near to each other.

blocks.text: You have spent this course learning to love the people around you: your neighbors, your family, and your church family. This lesson looks at the love that holds your closest relationships together. It is called covenant love, and it starts with the way God has already loved you.

blocks.alt: A husband handing his wife a chisel beside a rough block of marble, where a figure is beginning to emerge from the stone

blocks.title: The Marble and the Chisel
blocks.text:
In The Meaning of Marriage, Kathy Keller writes, "Most people, when they are looking for a spouse, are looking for a finished statue when they should be looking for a wonderful block of marble. Not so you can create the kind of person you want, but rather because you see what kind of person Jesus is making." Nobody you love is finished, and neither are you. Love begins with the willingness to look at a rough block of stone and see what Jesus is making in it.

Tim Keller adds that marriage exposes the rough edges in your own character. So picture marriage like this: you hand the other person your chisel, and they hand you theirs. You let them see your pride and selfishness, and you trust God to use them to shape you. A chisel in loving hands is patient and careful, and it is never a license to wound. That is what marriage is: two people willing to see something good in each other, pass the chisel, and trust each other with it.
That kind of trust does not come naturally. Most of us protect ourselves and keep score. The courage to hand someone your chisel comes from knowing how God has already loved you.
8.1 - When you look at the people closest to you, do you tend to see a finished statue you are measuring or a block of marble Jesus is shaping? What makes it hard for you to hand someone your chisel?
Covenant Love Starts with God

A covenant is a binding promise, and in every covenant with His people, God goes first. When God made His covenant with Abram, Abram cut a heifer, a goat, and a ram in half and laid the pieces in rows. Then a deep sleep fell on him, and in the dark "a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces" (Genesis 15:17). Only God, pictured by the fire, walked the path, taking the whole weight of the promise on Himself. At the cross, Jesus did the same for you. He paid for your sin before you did anything, and He called His death the "new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20).

Every close relationship runs on one of two agreements. A contract says, "I will, if you will." It keeps score and lasts only as long as the other person performs. A covenant says, "I will, even when." It rests on a promise, so it holds on the hard days. Tap through the Closer to God Triangle to see where that kind of love comes from.
Two people do not grow close by trying harder. They grow close as each one draws near to God. You give covenant love because you have first received it.
8.2 - In one close relationship, where are you keeping score: "I will, if you will"? What would "I will, even when" look like there this week?
Marriage: Christ's Love on Display

Paul calls marriage a profound mystery that points to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31-32). Every Christian marriage is a small billboard of that love: two imperfect people held by a faithful God. Paul begins with a word for every Christian: "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21). Before anyone talks about roles, everyone bows low before Jesus.

Paul asks wives to submit to their husbands "as to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:22) and to respect them (Ephesians 5:33). Biblical submission is not inferiority, silence, passivity, or following someone into sin. It is honoring and helping a husband under Jesus. Then Paul gives his longest words to husbands, and they may be the hardest of all.
Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,

Jesus did not wait for His bride to become lovely before He loved her. He gave Himself for her while she was still wandering. So a husband's leadership is measured by his sacrifice, not his control. If you promised you would die for her, you can lay down your pride for her today. Go first in serving, first in saying "I was wrong," and first in giving up your comfort for her good.

Because two sinners share one home, forgiveness is the oxygen of a Christian marriage. It sounds like, "I was wrong. Will you forgive me?" and "I forgive you." When you remember how much God has forgiven you (Matthew 18:21-35), you can stop keeping score. In Christ, people change and marriages grow. Marriage is a blessing, but only Jesus can be your ultimate satisfaction.

blocks.title: What covenant love is not
content: Covenant love is patient with ordinary weakness and ordinary hard days. It is not a promise to stay in danger. Ephesians 5 calls a husband to lay down his life, never to control, threaten, or harm, and biblical submission never means following someone into sin or accepting abuse. God never asks you to cover for someone who is hurting you or your children, and keeping your promises does not make you responsible for another person's sin.

If someone is harming, threatening, or controlling you, please tell a pastor or another safe, trusted person and get help. If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or your local emergency number. In the United States you can also call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

blocks.text: 8.3 - If you are married, where do you need to lay down your pride, ask forgiveness, or serve first this week? If you are not married, where can you practice covenant love in a close friendship or your church family?
Every Season Can Be Faithful

Maybe you are single, dating, or engaged. Maybe you are divorced, widowed, raising children on your own, blending two families, or in a hard marriage. God does not treat any of these seasons as a waiting room. Jesus never married, and He lived the most complete human life ever lived. Paul, who was also unmarried, called singleness a gift with a special freedom for "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:7, 35).

The deepest marriage in Ephesians 5 is Christ and the church, and if you belong to Jesus, you are part of the bride He gave Himself for. The triangle works in every relationship: as you and the other person each draw near to God, you draw near to each other. Your worth is not measured by your relationship status.
8.4 - What is hardest about the season of life you are in right now? What would faithfulness look like in it this week, instead of waiting for a different season?
Lesson 8 Review

Marriage is not finding a finished statue. It is two people who see what Jesus is making in each other, pass the chisel, and trust each other with it. That trust grows from covenant love, which God always gives first. A contract says, "I will, if you will," but a covenant says, "I will, even when." As two people draw near to God, they draw near to each other. In the next lesson, you will learn how to protect that triangle when temptation pulls you away from God.
